\section{MBR Decoding and Task-Specific Interactions}\label{app:mbr_discussion}

\paragraph{Connection to MBR decoding.}
Our selection strategies instantiate minimum Bayes risk (MBR) decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling, muller2021understanding}: each selects $\hat{y} = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} U(y_i, y_j)$ with utility $U$ defined by SJ, EM, or entity overlap.
Despite MBR's success in machine translation \cite{freitag2022high} and its extension to summarization, code generation, and captioning \cite{jinnai2024mbr}, all variants fail here because the utility functions correlate with F1 at the instance level but not within a single instance---the mathematical essence of the correlation-selection gap.
\citet{eikema2025structured} study structure-conditional MBR decoding and find that standard utility functions degrade on structured outputs---consistent with our finding that consensus-proximity selection fails in IE despite its success in machine translation.

\paragraph{Task-specific decoding interactions.}
The free-form ablation reveals divergent behavior across tasks.
On RE, LP selection flips from $-0.68$~pp (constrained) to $+1.69$~pp (free-form; preliminary, single RE benchmark), a reversal that spans all 7 relation types and is driven by selective variance reallocation ($p{<}0.0001$).
The win/loss ratio shifts from 36:59 (constrained) to 45:45 (free-form), with the gains concentrated on relation-dense instances (mean 3.3 gold relations).
This interaction does not generalize to NER, where selection remains negligible under both regimes.
This ablation uses a single seed (seed${=}42$); whether the RE reversal replicates across seeds and generalizes to other RE benchmarks warrants further investigation.
The non-tied subset ($n{=}210$) is partially reshuffled under free-form decoding: Jaccard similarity between the constrained and free-form non-tied sets is 0.472, indicating that 87 instances newly gain LP discrimination while others lose it, yielding a $3{\times}$ increase in within-instance LP range for the newly non-tied subset.
Despite this reshuffling, aggregate NER selection gains remain negligible---score compression is not a fixed property of specific instances but rather a pervasive regime that shifts across instances without producing net selection improvement.
Free-form decoding also slightly improves quality estimation (NER VC $\rho$: 0.379$\to$0.409), though this does not translate to selection gains.

\section{LP Selection Failure Stability}\label{app:lp_failure_stability}

We analyze RE LP selection failures across three random seeds (constrained decoding, $N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$, Qwen3-8B) to assess whether failures are systematic or stochastic.

\paragraph{Pairwise overlap.}
LP selection failures (instances where LP-selected F1 $<$ greedy F1) show moderate cross-seed stability: the average pairwise Jaccard similarity is 0.42 (range: 0.38--0.46), indicating that failures are partially systematic---driven by instance complexity---but not fully deterministic.
The 3-way intersection contains 34 instances (27.9\% of any-seed failures), confirming a stable failure core.

\paragraph{Instance complexity drives failure.}
Table~\ref{tab:stable_failures} stratifies instances by failure stability.
Stable failures (all 3 seeds) involve more gold relations (2.12 vs.\ 1.62 for never-fail instances) and higher greedy F1 (0.688 vs.\ 0.429), indicating that LP mis-selects on instances where the model already performs well---precisely the instances where selection would be most valuable.
Failure rate increases monotonically with gold relation count: 4.3\% at 1 relation, 20.7\% at 3 relations, 26.2\% at 6 relations.

Signal rankings are highly stable across seeds: Kendall's $W{=}1.000$ for NER at $N{=}8$ (both models), dropping only to $W{=}0.956$ at $N{=}16$ where SJ and VC converge (Table~\ref{tab:ranking-stability}).
Doubling $N$ reduces cross-seed $\sigma$ by 32\% on NER and 24\% on RE (Table~\ref{tab:sigma-comparison}), with the largest reductions for SJ ($-43\%$ NER) and EM ($-59\%$ NER), confirming that additional samples stabilize structural signals more than LP.

\section{Cross-Dataset OOD Analysis}\label{app:ood}

To test whether confidence signals generalize under domain shift, we evaluate models on out-of-distribution data: a SciERC-trained model applied to CoNLL instances (wider$\to$narrower schema) and vice versa (Table~\ref{tab:ood}).

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Cross-dataset OOD quality estimation (Spearman $\rho$, Qwen3-8B, $N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$, seed${=}42$). SciERC$\to$CoNLL: SciERC-trained model on CoNLL instances ($n{=}2756$). CoNLL$\to$SciERC: CoNLL-trained model on SciERC instances ($n{=}529$, excluded from conclusions due to catastrophic model failure). In-domain $\rho$ from Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation} (same model, same seed). \textsuperscript{***}$p{<}0.001$, \textsuperscript{*}$p{<}0.05$.}
\label{tab:ood}
\begin{tabular}{l ccc ccc}
\toprule
 & \multicolumn{3}{c}{\textbf{SciERC$\to$CoNLL}} & \multicolumn{3}{c}{\textbf{CoNLL$\to$SciERC}} \\
\cmidrule(lr){2-4} \cmidrule(lr){5-7}
Signal & $\rho$ & In-dom. & $\Delta$ & $\rho$ & In-dom. & $\Delta$ \\
\midrule
VC & .469\textsuperscript{***} & .379 & +.090 & +.105\textsuperscript{*} & .379 & $-$.274 \\
SJ & .378\textsuperscript{***} & .360 & +.018 & $-$.186\textsuperscript{***} & .360 & $-$.546 \\
EM & .300\textsuperscript{***} & .295 & +.005 & $-$.202\textsuperscript{***} & .295 & $-$.497 \\
FK & .285\textsuperscript{***} & .267 & +.018 & $-$.070 & .267 & $-$.337 \\
LP & .246\textsuperscript{***} & .205 & +.041 & $-$.152\textsuperscript{***} & .205 & $-$.357 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Wider-to-narrower schema transfer.}
When the SciERC-trained model (6 NER types) is applied to CoNLL (4 types), all signals remain significant ($p{<}0.001$) and structural signals improve over their in-domain levels (same model, seed${=}42$, $N{=}8$; in-domain $\rho$ from Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}): VC reaches $\rho{=}0.469$ (in-domain $0.379$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.090$), SJ $\rho{=}0.378$ (in-domain $0.360$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.018$), and FK $\rho{=}0.285$ (in-domain $0.267$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.018$).
The wider training schema subsumes CoNLL's narrower schema, so the model produces reasonable outputs even out-of-domain (greedy F1${=}0.522$), and structural signals benefit from the simpler target schema's reduced output ambiguity.

\paragraph{Narrower-to-wider schema transfer (excluded).}
The reverse direction is excluded from our conclusions due to catastrophic model failure, not signal failure.
The CoNLL-trained model recognizes only 4 news entity types (PER, ORG, LOC, MISC) and has no relation extraction capability; when applied to SciERC's 6 scientific entity types and 7 relation types, the model cannot produce meaningful structured outputs (greedy NER F1${=}0.009$, RE F1${=}0.001$).
Under this regime, most signals flip to negative or near-zero correlations (Table~\ref{tab:ood}); only VC retains weak positive correlation ($\rho{=}0.105$, $p{=}0.016$).
These negative correlations reflect the model systematically generating confident but incorrect outputs---a capability failure analogous to WNUT-17 (\S\ref{sec:qe_results}), not evidence against signal utility.

\paragraph{Asymmetry interpretation.}
The directional asymmetry is driven by schema coverage: wider$\to$narrower preserves signal utility because the SciERC model's 6-type schema subsumes CoNLL's 4 types, while narrower$\to$wider fails because the CoNLL model lacks the entity and relation types required by SciERC.
This extends the capability boundary identified on WNUT-17 to the domain-shift setting: confidence signals require sufficient model capability as a prerequisite, and results from the CoNLL$\to$SciERC direction should not be interpreted as evidence of signal degradation under domain shift.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about EMNLP 2026 ARR submission requirements:

## Anonymity Requirements

Following the ACL and ARR policies, there is no anonymity period requirement. However, the reviewing process will continue to be double-blind, with reviewers not seeing authors, nor will authors see reviewers. Additionally, papers must not include authors' names and affiliations, and self-references that reveal the authors' identities must be avoided.

## Important Policy Details

Authors will be given the option through ARR to make their anonymized submitted articles publicly visible. Beginning with the February 15, 2024 ARR deadlines, there is no anonymity period or limitation on posting or discussing non-anonymous preprints while the work is under peer review, though the new policy incentivizes anonymous submissions by special paper awards and priority in acceptance decisions for borderline papers.

## Format and Submission

The search results indicate that both long and short paper submissions should follow all of the ARR submission requirements, but the specific page limit information for EMNLP 2026 is not detailed in these results. For precise page limit requirements, you may need to check the full ARR Call for Papers document directly.

Based on the search results, I found the research you're looking for. Bryan Eikema, Anna Rutkiewicz, and Mario Giulianelli published a 2025 paper in the Proceedings of the 2025 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing.

The paper is titled "Structure-Conditional Minimum Bayes Risk Decoding." Here's what the research focuses on:

**Main Contribution:**
The work introduces three lightweight adaptations to the utility function, designed to make MBR more sensitive to structural variability in the outcome space.

**Methodology:**
The researchers curated a dataset capturing three representative types of latent structure—dialogue act, emotion, and response structure (e.g., a sentence, a paragraph, or a list)—and proposed two metrics to evaluate the structural optimality of MBR.

**Key Findings:**
- Common similarity-based utility functions fall short by these metrics, while the proposed adaptations considerably improve structural optimality
- The approaches were evaluated on real-world instruction-following benchmarks (AlpacaEval and MT-Bench), showing that increased structural sensitivity improves generation quality by up to 13.7 percentage points in win rate

The paper addresses a limitation of standard MBR decoding in open-ended tasks like dialogue and instruction-following, where the model's output space is less constrained than in machine translation.

content.content:
# EMNLP 2026 Submission Requirements

## Page Limits
- **Long Papers:** 8 pages of content
- **Short Papers:** 4 pages of content
- **Camera-ready versions:** +1 additional page allowed (9 pages for long papers, 5 pages for short papers) to address reviewer feedback

## Anonymity Requirements
The document states: "Following the ACL and ARR policies, there is no anonymity period requirement." However, the reviewing process itself maintains double-blind review—"Reviewers will not see authors, nor will authors see reviewers."

## Required Sections & Content Elements
Papers must include:
- **Limitations section** (explicitly required per ARR standards)
- **Ethics considerations** per the responsible NLP research checklist
- **Disclosure of any conflicts of interest** following ACL's Disclosure Policy
- Compliance with the "ACL Policy on Publication Ethics"

## Format & Submission Standards
- Follow all "ARR submission requirements" regarding formatting
- Use official paper templates (reference to submission portal for specific templates)
- Include proper citations and comparisons per guidelines
- Supplementary materials (appendices, software, data) are optional

## Author List & Authorship
- During commitment phase: "modification of author list (addition/deletion of authors) is not allowed"
- Author order modifications are permitted during commitment

## Writing Assistance
AI writing assistance is explicitly permitted per conference policy.

## Dual Submission Policy
"Dual submissions are not allowed" according to ARR standards referenced in the call.
